title: Who shaped the early newspaper page
bodyMd: Many histories of the early newspaper treat its editor as the central figure, the person whose views filled its columns. Historian Mireille Achterberg does not dispute that editors wrote the lead essays. But after studying the account books of eleven print shops in the eighteenth-century port of Kessling, she argues that what readers actually saw on the page owed more to the compositors, the workers who set the type by hand. A page had to be filled exactly before the press could run, so compositors routinely shortened letters from readers, dropped paragraphs that would not fit, and filled any gaps with shipping notices of their own choosing. The account books, which paid compositors by the column, record many of these decisions in their margins.

Historian Mireille Achterberg does not dispute that editors wrote the lead essays, but after studying the account books of eleven print shops in the eighteenth-century port of Kessling, she argues that what readers actually saw on the page owed more to the compositors, the workers who set type by hand. Because a page had to be filled exactly before the press could run, compositors routinely shortened readers' letters, dropped paragraphs that would not fit, and filled gaps with shipping notices they chose themselves. The account books, which paid compositors by the column, record many of these decisions in their margins.
